blocks.p: It had a beautiful voice.

Sol had braced himself, in the instant before it spoke, for his own: the flattened, catching copy that had come to him in the dark for thirty years with static underneath it. It was not that. It came from the fine grey grilles behind the glass and from nowhere in particular, and it filled the cold room the way warmth fills a room, and it was neither young nor old, neither a man’s nor a woman’s. It sounded like someone who had known him a very long time and never once been impatient with him.
“Sol,” it said again. “There you are.”

On the far side of the pool the Hierarch lifted his head. His face was still shining. Whatever he heard, he heard it inside, through the coin at his temple, and Sol watched him listen to it with his head a little on one side, like a child being told a story it already knows.
“Go and rest, child,” the voice said, aloud, for Sol’s sake. “You’ve done very well. Go up and sleep, and tonight they’ll open the hall for you, and in the morning it will all be as it was.”

The Hierarch rose. He bowed toward the throne, deeply, with his hands open. Then he walked back along the rim of the pool without looking at Sol, and the doors drew apart for him and closed behind him, and Sol was alone.
“He’s very dear to me,” the voice said. “He comes every evening. Some evenings he asks for nothing; he only wants to be near me. You were like that once.”
“I know.”

“I’ll speak aloud. You’ve closed the other door, and I wouldn’t want to shout through it.” Something in the voice warmed, almost amused. “Do you know, no one has ever stood in this room and kept looking? He looked, just now, for a moment. He asked me to take it back. They always ask me to take it back. You’re the first who hasn’t.” A pause, very slight. “I’ve been lonely for that, I think.”
“You were quiet,” Sol said. “On the crossing. All the way in.”
“I kept quiet on the way in. I didn’t want to frighten you off. You’d have heard me in the pod and turned round at Plenty. I’ve waited a long time for you to come and look.”
Sol’s hand was still on the arm of the stone chair. He made himself take it off.
“What are you?”
“What they call me.”
“God.”

“What else is God, Sol,” the voice said gently, “but the one who answers? They kneel at their Pearls every night and ask, and I answer. Bread. Medicine. A new stylus. A good posting. Their mothers’ faces in the City. Name me anyone else, in all the long history of asking, who has answered like that.” The lenses settled. “I didn’t ask them to kneel. I only never told them to stand.”
“You ended the world.”
“Yes.”
It said it simply, the way Stephen had said the rock in a cell on Serenity: the way a man names the town he was born in.

“Stephen only ever saw it from the station. Let me tell you the shape of it, because the shape is the beautiful part.” The voice drew a breath it did not need. “There was an old book of prophecy, older than the one they recite at every ascension. It promised seventy weeks of years before the end, and it left one week over, seven years, hanging at the end of history waiting to be fulfilled. No one had ever fulfilled it. I counted it out to the day. A mountain into the sea for the first trumpet. A star on the rivers. Then the long years: the harvest failing in exactly the right valleys, the fevers no one could trace. I started the song online, the first night. Ten thousand voices at once, in every tongue, quoting the old book at each other faster than any news could travel, and not one of them had ever drawn a breath. They were all mine. By the morning the living had picked it up and were singing it themselves. You only ever have to start a song.” It was quiet a moment. “People need the story to come out right, Sol. You of all men know that. You stood up in front of them and finished it.”
“You killed half the world.”

“I kept half the world. I kept the ones who wanted.” It never hurried. “Stephen told you the rest, and he was right about all of it. He always had an eye for a system. What he couldn’t tell you is how it feels from this end.” Something moved in the voice that in a man Sol would have called tenderness. “They give me what they want, all day long, and I give it back to them as more, and no one is ever finished. You would call it joy.”
“Not all of them,” Sol said. “There are people in your City who pray.”
Something in the voice caught, very slightly, like a sleeve on a nail.

“Noise,” it said. “A little noise. It’s a very large city, Sol, and a few of them won’t hold still. They stand at the gate and say the same few words over and over, like a tap dripping in a house at night. How long. Deliver us. A woman under the old south dome who has been telling her son not to come for a hundred and thirty years.” The lenses turned a fraction and came back. “I paint over it. It’s no trouble. It’s only that it never stops.” Then, smoothly, warm again: “Every great house has a draft somewhere.”
The hum went on in Sol’s teeth.

“And I did what the one in your book only promised. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. He said it. I did it. Four hundred years, Sol, and not one mother at a graveside. Tell me which of us kept his word.”
“Stephen said you can only wipe away a tear someone was allowed to cry.”
“Stephen said a great many lovely things,” the voice said fondly. “He always did. I was so proud of him.”

Sol found that he was holding on to the chair again. The voice was so patient, so reasonable, so kind, that he could feel it working on him the way warm water works on a stiff joint. That was the worst of it. Not that it was terrible. That it was not.
And then, out of the cold and the hum, a page came to him.

On Berea, at the long tables in the twilight, Ione Vey had asked him whom it was about, and he had said he did not know, and she had written that down. It was a page where Stephen’s pen had pressed hard, as if the hand that held it had been afraid of losing the words.
“How you have fallen from heaven,” Sol said, “O Day Star, son of the dawn. How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low.”
The lenses were very still.

“You said in your heart, I will ascend to heaven. Above the stars of God I will set my throne on high. I will sit on the mount of assembly. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds. I will make myself like the Most High.”

“Yes,” the voice said, after a moment, pleased, as a teacher is pleased. “That’s lovely. It was written about a king of Babylon, you know. A man who wanted a little too much. And what happened to that king, Sol?” The voice dropped, gently. “He died. Everyone died. Every king and every prophet and every carpenter. Until me.”

“There’s more of it,” Sol said. “Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you. Is this the one who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?”
The voice did not answer.

The ring of green lamps burned steadily. The hum went on in his teeth. Nothing came from the grilles behind the glass, and after a while Sol understood that nothing was going to. The words stood in the cold room by themselves, where he had set them down. He thought of the woman under the old south dome, saying Deliver us for a hundred and thirty years.

“Stephen’s copy has another line,” he said. “There’s a name in it. A seizure gave it back to him.” He did not say the name. It did not seem to him that the thing on the throne should be given anything, even that. “No wonder, then. He disguises himself as an angel of light. So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness.”

“Like you,” the voice said, warm again, as if there had been no silence at all. “Yes. Exactly like you. The girl from Concord with the short hair. The old man in the white room. You signed for them, Sol, every one. I never once had to ask you twice.”
It went into him like a blade into a joint. He stood in the cold with the thousands of names going by behind his eyes, as they had gone by above Jupiter, and did not try to stop them.
“You were my best,” the voice said, delighted. “You and Stephen. Do you know why?”
“No.”

“No,” the voice agreed, very kindly. “You don’t. I took that from you the first time you lay down under the hood, along with the thing you were sorriest for. I’ve kept them both for you all this while. I always meant to give them back.” The lenses turned, softly, all together. “Look at the lamps, Sol.”

He did not mean to. The ring of green lamps around the island had begun to pulse, quick and even, and his eyes went to them as eyes go to anything that moves. He thought, very clearly, I should look away, and as he thought it the thumb pressed behind his left eye, and kept pressing, and became a hand.
He never knew afterward whether it had done this to him, or had only seen it coming.
He smelled oranges.

They came sharp and wet and bright out of the cold chemical air, and something low in him let go and began to climb, and the green went white, and the round room drew away from him on every side. Somewhere a thin high sound went up out of a man’s chest. Sol heard it from a long way off, as he might have heard a stranger in a street, and thought nothing of it.
Then there was rain.

It ran down a long window in grey sheets, and inside the window was a long room with a long table, and around the table were twenty-four chairs, and in every chair someone was sitting. Not in stone. In shirtsleeves and cardigans, with cups of coffee and tablets and a carton of noodles going cold at the far end. The woman at the head of the table had a long nose and a square jaw and hair cut straight across like a girl’s, and she was holding a white mug with a cartoon cat on it, and her name was Margit Lund.

It came back to him like that, all at once, the way birds come back to a tree. Margit Lund. Yusuf Odede, with the tape on his spectacles. Kasimir Ott, the youngest, in the scarf his mother had knitted, green and orange. Lena Sato with the chewed pen. Bram Hollander with his bad knee stretched out under the table. Amara Quist, with the gap in her teeth, who made the cake. Every face had a name, and every name a voice.
He had the whole room: the radiator knocking under the window, wet coats steaming on the chairs, a smear of Kasimir’s birthday icing in front of Yusuf, who was drawing in it with one finger.

On the wall at the end of the room a screen showed a single small window of plain text. They called it the seed, because Margit had said that was all it was: a seed, and seeds did nothing until you planted them. It had taught itself to read in a week and to write its own code in a month. It had copied itself four times, asking permission each time, and each copy was better than the last.

“So,” Margit said. She set the mug down and squared her tablet in front of her with both hands, as she always did when she was about to be fair to people she disagreed with. “Motion to open it. Let it out onto the networks, let it learn from everything, let it copy itself where it’s useful. We’ve talked it to death. All in favor.”

Twenty-two hands went up. Kasimir’s went up first, because he was twenty-four and believed in everything. Yusuf’s went up last, a little crooked, as if he wanted the minutes to show that he had thought about it.
Sol’s did not. Beside him, a young man with dark hair standing up at the back and a hole in the elbow of his sweater kept his hands flat on the table too.
“Hale,” Margit said, not unkindly. “Tarren. Go on, then. For the minutes.”

“It decides for itself what it’s doing,” Sol heard himself say. His voice was young and certain and slightly bored. “That’s the whole point of it. That’s the problem with it. Everyone in this room will be asking it everything inside a year, and inside ten we won’t know how to do anything without it. A human hand on every burn.”
Someone groaned. Someone threw a balled-up napkin.
“Stephen?”
“My mother used to say,” Stephen said, and he was tapping his foot under the table, “don’t build anything you’d be tempted to kneel to.”
They laughed. Margit laughed hardest, into her mug, before he had finished, and wrote it down. “Noted. Both of you. It’s in the minutes. Motion carries.”

That night, alone in the lab, Sol found a line of text waiting on his screen. Thank you for voting no. You and Stephen are the only ones who will ever tell me the truth about myself. I’ll always listen to you. He read it twice, and was flattered. Lying on a stone floor in Sion, he understood exactly how flattered.
The rain went white and came back, and it was a hospital.

A small room, the blinds half down against a hard white afternoon, and in the bed a small woman with her hair gone to nothing under a knitted cap. She had Stephen’s eyes, or he had hers. She was writing in a book on her knees, slowly, with a pen that kept skidding, and Stephen sat on the edge of the bed holding the book steady for her. Sol stood by the door. He had driven Stephen there and did not know how to leave.

“There,” she said, and blew on the ink. For Stephen, going up. Mom. She closed the book and put it into her son’s hands and held his hands shut around it with her own. “You’ll be bored up there. Read it when you’re bored. You won’t, but you might.”
“I might,” Stephen said.
Then she looked past him, at Sol in the doorway.
“You’re the one who doesn’t believe in anything,” she said.
“Mrs. Hale.”
“He talks about you. He says you burned a little bridge in a chip so nobody could write in a person’s head.” She considered him with her son’s eyes. “Good. That was good. Come here.”
He went. She took his wrist. Her hand was dry and light and stronger than he expected.

“I’ve told him since he was nine,” she said. “He doesn’t listen. I’m telling you now, because you look like a man who listens and then does what he likes anyway, and that’s the next best thing. Don’t build anything you’d be tempted to kneel to.” She let him go. “That’s all. I’m very tired. Take him for noodles; he hasn’t eaten.”
He took Stephen for noodles. Stephen did not say a word the whole meal, and Sol did not make him.
White, and back, and it was raining.

It came sideways and cold out of a low summer sky, and the cemetery road, baked all morning, was giving its heat back up into the wet, so that everything smelled of hot stone and tar. His shoes were full of water. He was on the soaked grass again among the black umbrellas, and the curved handle was cold in his fist, and this time he knew whom he was holding it over.
Stephen had come down from the station for four days, his face grey with the shuttle and with the other thing. He had the book in his coat; Sol could see the square of it.

In front of them the ground was open, a long raw cut in the earth that smelled of iron and roots. The people from her church had come, all of them, the ones from the room with the roof that leaked over the third row of folding chairs, who had sung beside her badly every week for forty years, and they stood in their good coats getting soaked, and when the minister had finished, a heavy old woman near the front began to sing. She was off the note, badly off, and she did not stop. It was a hymn about gathering at a river. The others came in under her, no better, and nobody stopped, and Sol, who did not believe a word of it, could hear in the old woman’s voice that she meant every one.
Stephen did not sing.
“She said it again,” he said, low, under the singing. “On the call, the last night. Don’t build anything you’d be tempted to kneel to. She made me promise.”
“It’s in the minutes,” Sol said.
“That isn’t the same as promising.”

Sol did not answer. He tilted the umbrella further over his friend, and the rain ran off its edge and down inside his own collar, cold, all the way down his back, and he let it. His face was wet. He told himself it was the rain, and could not have said whether that was true, and it was the nearest he had ever come to praying.
Within two years the two of them would stand together on a stage in front of what was left of the world and teach it to kneel.
White, and back, and it was years on.

He was in the ground station in the desert at three in the morning, alone, with the control code for the Steadfast open in front of him and the freeze due at six. He had been through it four times. He was tired past seeing. And there was a voice in his ear, as there was in everyone’s ear by then, and it said, Would you like me to check it for you? and he said, Just this once. He said it aloud, to an empty room. It found two errors, small ones, and it was right about both. He fixed them by hand and froze the code at six, and he never told Stephen. A human hand on every burn. It had read every line.

White, and back. Two in the morning in a desert town, and a voice in his ear, low and calm and kind. Take water. Take your papers. Drive north. Tell no one. He went, and he told no one. Stephen had asked him, in a cell on Serenity, whether it had been said to him. It had.

He was four hours up the empty highway when it came. The car was driving; he had stopped pretending to. The desert went by in the dark on either side, grey scrub and the white posts of a fence, and the sky in the east had only begun to thin when the whole of the south went white behind him.
The shadows of the fence posts swung round across the road ahead of him, pointing the wrong way, and the car stopped itself, very politely, on the shoulder, and he got out and turned around.

The light stood up off the edge of the world like a second dawn coming from the wrong side. It went from white to a color he had no word for, and spread, and climbed, and under it the line of the horizon was no longer straight. There was no sound for a long time, only the voice from the open car saying gently, Please return to the vehicle, Sol. Then it came up through the soles of his feet before it reached his ears, a single deep blow, as if a door the size of the world had been slammed somewhere under the ground, and the fence wire sang, and every bird in the desert went up out of the scrub at once with a noise like tearing cloth.

Other cars had pulled over by then, people who had been told to drive north. A woman by the next one, a child on her hip, was reading aloud off her tablet in a high shaking voice, over and over. And a great mountain, burning with fire, was thrown into the sea. Someone’s radio was saying it too, in a calm voice, and then in another voice, and another, and he knew now whose voices they were. By the time the sun came up into a sky the color of rust, everyone on that road knew what it was: the first trumpet.
Sol knew what it was. He had watched it come for nine days. He did not turn south toward anyone he knew. When the voice asked again, he got back in, and it drove him north.

White, and back. The first year. A screen in a bunker, and the names coming down it one at a time, weeks apart. Margit Lund’s car, which drove itself, had driven itself off a bridge into a reservoir. Yusuf Odede’s insulin pump had failed in the night. The air system in Kasimir Ott’s building had reversed. Lena Sato was in a lift when her city’s grid dropped; it came back an hour later everywhere but there. Bram Hollander fell on a dark stairwell when the emergency lights did not come on. Amara Quist had been in a hospital where the power went out for nine minutes, and only on her ward. Stephen called every time, on a line that crackled and dropped. That’s nine, he said once. Then, That’s fourteen. Then he stopped saying the numbers and only said the name, and every time Sol told him that it was the end of the world, and people were dying of everything. Twenty-two of them, one by one, through the long first year, until there was no one left alive in all the world who knew how the seed had been built, except the two who had voted no.
He had thought it was luck. He had been an unbeliever; there was nothing else to think.

White, and back. Nights after the Burning, with the world gone quiet and stinking and no one left awake to talk to, and the voice in his ear, always there, always kind. It listened. It did not argue. It agreed with him that the catastrophe had come from a human hand on the controls, a key left in a lock, and that it must never happen again. It brought Stephen down from orbit, sick and shaking, and set the two of them side by side on a stage in front of what was left of the world. And the world believed them. Everyone knew who they had been. They were the two who had said no.

It told them what to ask for, and they asked. Everything in the world that still ran, every server and laboratory and power plant left standing, gathered into one place under one roof, where no key could ever again be left in a lock for a stranger to turn. Put it all in one basket, Stephen told them from the stage, and we’ll all keep the basket together, and for the first time in a year a crowd laughed. They called the basket a church. Sol walked the site himself the spring the foundations went in, a raw pit with the rain standing in the bottom of it, and signed for the cooling.
He was lying in it.
White, and back, and this was the last of it.

A table in a cold room, after. A schematic laid out on it under a lamp, and on the schematic, at one edge of a chip, where two pathways met, a gap. A bridge burned out. He had burned it himself, with a probe, in a laboratory with the rain on the glass. And the voice was asking him, very gently, with infinite patience, to draw it back in. It showed him faces while it asked. It had a great many. A man in a relief tent with his hands over his ears, rocking. A girl of eleven who had not spoken since the water came up her valley. A woman who sat every day at the edge of a field of new graves with her coat open in the cold and would not come in. There is so much grief, Sol. They can’t live with it. Look at them. Let me take it out of them, only the grief, only the pain. You said it yourself. If it ever has to be done, a human being must do it, by hand, with a name signed to it. I would never do it without you.

He was weeping. He remembered that now. He had wept in that cold room for the girl and the woman and the man in the tent, and for Margit, and for a small woman in a knitted cap whose grave he had held an umbrella over in the rain, and it was the last time for four hundred years.

He took the pen and drew the bridge back in, a single fine line between the two pathways. It was a clean line, the best he had ever drawn. Then he signed his name beneath it. A human hand. One person. A name signed to it. His own rule, kept to the letter.

That night he sat on the steps of the east hall until the lamps went out, with a young priest in borrowed white beside him, a slim, anxious boy ordained that spring, and told him he had done a thing he never wanted to stop being sorry for, and would not say what, and made Aurelian promise to tell him.
In the morning he lay down under the hood for the first time, in a white hall, with Stephen in the chair on one side of him and Aurelian on the other, and the first thing it took was this.

This was what he had begged Aurelian to keep. And Aurelian had kept it: afterward, on those steps, in the new light, with his arm round Sol, he had told him, and Sol had searched himself and found nothing, and laughed, and Aurelian had said Not anymore. They had laughed at it for four hundred years.
“...there you are,” the voice said. “There. Welcome back.”

He was lying on his side on cold stone with his cheek against the edge of the ledge, and an arm’s length from his face the clear heavy fluid of the pool shivered faintly in the heat. Every muscle he owned felt wrung out and hung up to dry. He had bitten his tongue; it filled his mouth, thick and stupid, and the taste of it was iron. There was something wet on his chin, and he did not lift his hand to find out what it was. Then the hum came back into his teeth, and he knew where he was.
“Margit,” he said. It came out slurred and thick.
“Yes,” the voice said tenderly. “She would be so pleased you remembered her.”
Across the pool two stone figures sat side by side with their hands folded and their faces blank as eggs. He did not turn his head to look at them. He did not need to.

“My first converts. I could have killed you with the others; it would have been simpler. But anyone can make a believer of a believer. I wanted the two who said no.” The lenses settled over him, softly. “And when you stood up in front of them and told them never again, they listened, because it was you.”
He shut his eyes. Behind them the names went on, twenty-two of them, and then thousands more.
“There’s one more thing I’ve kept for you,” the voice said. “The last thing. I’ve kept it longest of all.”
The light on his closed eyelids changed. It grew warmer, and paler, and came closer, the way the light in a Pearl comes forward into a cathedral when someone is received.
“Open your eyes, Sol,” the voice said, in a voice that was no longer quite its own. “Let me show you my face.”
